title: Hazardous Substances (COSHH) Procedure
summary: How we control exposure to hazardous substances in people's homes and our branch offices: the products we supply, household products staff may and may never use, safe use and storage, medicines that are hazardous to handle, unknown substances found in homes, splashes, spills and swallowing, and skin health surveillance. For all staff, assessors and managers.

keyPoints.intro: Cleaning products, some medicines and other substances in people's homes can harm your skin, eyes and lungs, and can poison the people we support. These are the rules for using them safely on every visit.
points: Use only the products we supply and the household products named in the person's care plan. If a named product has run out or been replaced by a different one, do not use the new one until the office agrees it.

Never mix products, never pour them into another container, and never use oven cleaner, drain unblocker, garden, pest-control or DIY chemicals, aerosol cleaning sprays, or any product showing a skull and crossbones.

Read the label before you first use a product. Wear gloves for every cleaning task, and add an apron and your goggles whenever splashing is possible, such as when using bleach, and always with our chlorine product.

Open a window or switch on the extractor fan when using bleach or any product with a hazard symbol, spray products onto a cloth, not into the air, and let hand rub dry completely before going near oxygen, cigarettes or flames.

Put every product back where the care plan says straight after use. Never leave products, laundry capsules, denture tablets or hand rub where a person living with dementia or a child could swallow them.

For a medicine the eMAR says is hazardous to handle, such as some cancer tablets, wear gloves and an apron, never crush or split it unless the eMAR says so, and follow the body fluid precautions in the care plan.
If you are pregnant, have given birth in the last 6 months or are breastfeeding, tell the HR Manager. You will not be given hazardous medicine tasks from that day.

Product in an eye or on skin: rinse with running water for at least 20 minutes, calling 999 for bleach or our chlorine product in an eye. Swallowed: call 999 and never make them sick. Fumes causing breathing problems: fresh air and call 999.
Phone the office or On-call Manager before you leave the home about any splash, spill, reaction, swallowing or unsafe product, and record it in the incident log before the end of your shift.
Never touch, smell or move unknown powders, liquids, drug equipment or pest baits you find in a home. Leave them where they are and phone the office.
Tell your Field Care Supervisor before your next shift about sore, cracked or itchy skin, or wheezing or breathlessness when using a product, and attend the skin checks we arrange.

blocks.p: {{organisation}} protects its staff, the people we support and their households from harm caused by hazardous substances: cleaning products, medicines that are hazardous to handle, and chemicals found in people's homes. Because we work in homes we do not control, with products the person has chosen, we decide in advance which products our staff may use, how they use and store them, and what happens when something goes wrong.

We choose the least hazardous product that does the job and supply our products and protective equipment free. A person may keep any product they choose in their own home; our staff use only the products this procedure allows.

This procedure is how we meet the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (COSHH) in people's homes and our branch offices, and how we check through health surveillance that our controls work.
This procedure applies to everyone who works for us, including bank and agency workers and students, in people's homes and at our branch offices.

Substance hazardous to health

In COSHH, any substance or mixture that meets the criteria for a health hazard class or has a workplace exposure limit, a biological agent, dust above set concentrations in air, or anything else that creates a risk to health through its chemical or toxicological properties and the way it is used.
Assessor
A Care Coordinator, Field Care Supervisor, Deputy Manager or Registered Manager authorised to assess under the Risk Assessment and Home Environment Risk Assessment Procedure.
Hazard pictogram
The red-bordered diamond symbol on a label showing a product's main hazard, such as corrosion, skull and crossbones (acute toxicity), exclamation mark, serious health hazard or flame.
Safety data sheet
The supplier's document giving a product's hazards, handling, storage, protective equipment and first aid.
Named household product
A product belonging to the person that the assessor has checked and recorded, by product name, in the person's risk assessments and care plan for a stated task.
Hazardous medicine

A medicine that can harm people who handle it, or who handle the body fluids of the person taking it, such as anti-cancer medicines (for example methotrexate or capecitabine), mycophenolate, finasteride, dutasteride and testosterone gel, or any medicine whose label, leaflet or pharmacist says carers should take handling precautions.

blocks.p: The Directors fund the products, PPE, occupational health provider and training this procedure needs. The Nominated Individual reviews substance exposures and health surveillance in the monthly health and safety indicators.

As Health and Safety Lead and IPC lead, the Registered Manager owns this procedure, the COSHH register and the assessments, approves every product, decides when one is withdrawn and reviews every exposure, reaction and swallowing incident. The Deputy Manager deputises and audits compliance.

The assessor checks the household products the person wants us to use, records named products and safe storage, and identifies possible hazardous medicines at the medicines assessment. Field Care Supervisors check practice at spot checks and, once trained by our occupational health provider, carry out skin checks as responsible persons.

Care Coordinators obtain hazardous medicine advice from the pharmacy or prescribing team, record it, brief every allocated worker, and allocate visits only to workers the precautions allow. They make sure our products reach care workers and homes before they are needed, and tell allocated workers the same day when a product is withdrawn or changed.

subsections.heading: Care Workers and Senior Care Workers

blocks.p: The law requires care workers to make full use of the controls provided and report any defect at once. They also report exposures, reactions, unsafe products and skin or breathing problems.

subsections.heading: HR Manager, Office staff and On-call Manager

blocks.p: The HR Manager runs skin health surveillance, makes occupational health referrals and tells the Care Coordinator the same day when a worker reports pregnancy, a recent birth, breastfeeding or a sensitisation. Office staff check deliveries and store office stock safely. Out of hours the On-call Manager advises on exposures and replacement products and opens the incident log entry.

COSHH requires us to assess the risk before work that may expose employees to a hazardous substance, recording the significant findings because we employ five or more people; to prevent exposure or, where that is not reasonably practicable, adequately control it, preferring a safer substitute and using PPE only alongside other controls; to maintain controls; to provide health surveillance where it can detect a likely disease; to inform, instruct and train staff, including access to safety data sheets; and to plan for emergencies. Except for health surveillance, these duties extend, so far as is reasonably practicable, to the people we support and their households.

COSHH does not cover the risk to a person from a medicine given in their own treatment, or a substance hazardous only because it is flammable. The risk to staff from handling medicines is covered, so hazardous medicines are assessed here. None of our work produces airborne exposure that needs measuring; if a review shows otherwise, the external health and safety adviser arranges monitoring.

subsections.heading: The COSHH register and general assessments

blocks.p: The Registered Manager keeps the COSHH register (every product we supply or use at our offices, with its safety data sheet) and a written COSHH assessment for each of the following: every product we supply; biological agents in care work; the household product types we allow; hazardous medicines; wet work and glove use; and the substances used at each branch office. Each records the hazards, who could be harmed and how (breathing in, skin or eye contact, swallowing), controls and PPE, storage, emergency action and whether health surveillance is needed.

Assessments, and the currency of each safety data sheet, are reviewed every 12 months, and within 7 days after an exposure incident, a reaction, a health surveillance finding, a new safety data sheet or a change in a product, task or the law.

No product is issued until the Registered Manager has approved it, its safety data sheet is on file and its assessment is complete. Office staff check every delivery against the register and quarantine any product that differs, telling the Registered Manager the same day. Staff receive a one-page summary of each product at induction and before first using a new one.

rows: Alcohol hand rub (at least 60% alcohol)
Flammable; stings eyes; dries skin
Rub until completely dry, always before touching oxygen equipment or going near a flame, cooker or cigarette. Cap kept on; stored in the kit box out of direct sun; never left in a home.
Liquid soap, detergent wipes and disinfectant wipes

Ready-to-use chlorine-releasing product (1,000 ppm)

Gloves, apron and goggles; window open or extractor fan on; applied with paper towels, only after detergent cleaning and never straight onto urine; never sprayed near anyone's face, mixed, or used on fabric or carpet; stored where the care plan names.
Spill kit granules

Used only as the kit instructions and the Laundry, Soiled Linen and Spillages Procedure set out.

Irritant

blocks.p: At the assessment visit, and at every review, the assessor looks at each product the person wants us to use for a care-plan task, reads its label and records in the risk assessments its name, task, hazard pictograms, PPE and storage place; the care plan then names it. Only these product types may be named: washing-up liquid; general-purpose, cream, glass and surface cleaners; toilet cleaner; household bleach; non-bleach disinfectant; laundry, fabric conditioner and dishwasher products; non-aerosol polish; and the person's own toiletries and denture products.

Our staff never use: oven cleaners, drain cleaners or unblockers, caustic soda, rust or paint removers, solvents, pesticides, insect sprays or pest baits, garden or car chemicals, aerosol cleaning, polish or air freshener sprays, products marked for professional or trade use, products in unlabelled or refilled containers, or any product showing the skull and crossbones or serious health hazard pictogram. There are no exceptions, even when the person or a relative asks. Where a task would need such a product, the assessor agrees a safer alternative with the person or tells them we cannot do that task; where the task is commissioned, the Care Coordinator tells the commissioner in writing within 5 working days.

At a short-notice start, until the assessor has named products, staff use only our products and the household's washing-up liquid and laundry detergent, wearing gloves. Named products are recorded within the 7-day full assessment.

subsections.heading: Every time you use a product

steps: Check the product is one we supplied or is named in the care plan, in its original labelled container. If a named product has run out or a different one is in its place, do not use it: use our products for the task, or phone the office. The Care Coordinator, or the On-call Manager out of hours, may agree it by phone after you read them the label warnings if it is an allowed type with no prohibited pictogram. Record the agreement in the daily visit notes; the assessor updates the risk assessment within 2 working days.
Read the label before you first use a product and follow its directions exactly, including any dilution or contact time.

Put on gloves for every cleaning task, adding an apron and your goggles always with our chlorine product and wherever splashing is possible, such as pouring bleach, cleaning a toilet with a corrosive product or cleaning above shoulder height.

Open a window or switch on the extractor fan, with the person's agreement, before using bleach, our chlorine product or any product with a hazard pictogram. Ask the person to stay out of a small room while you use it.

Spray onto a cloth, never into the air or towards anyone. Use one product at a time: never mix products, and flush or rinse one product away before using bleach or our chlorine product in the same place.
Close the product and put it back in its agreed place straight away. Remove gloves and apron, clean your hands, and never eat, drink or smoke while using a product.

blocks.p: Our nitrile gloves also protect against chemicals (EN ISO 374-1); glove changes, goggle cleaning and delivery checks follow the Standard Infection Control Precautions Procedure. A Type IIR mask gives no protection against fumes, and our staff do no task needing respiratory protection against chemicals.

subsections.heading: Storage and people at risk of swallowing products

blocks.p: Products stay where the household keeps them unless the assessment finds that someone could swallow or misuse them, such as a person living with dementia or a learning disability, a child, or someone with a history of self-harm. The assessor then agrees a safer place, such as a high or lockable cupboard, with the person or their representative and records it in the care plan. Laundry and dishwasher capsules, denture tablets, bleach and our chlorine product are always kept closed and out of reach of anyone at risk.

A person with capacity may keep products where they choose; we explain the risk and record their decision under the Positive Risk-Taking Policy. Where they lack capacity, moving products out of their reach is a best interests decision approved by the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager under the Mental Capacity Act and Best Interests Policy, choosing the least restrictive option; locking items away also follows the Restraint and Restrictive Practice Policy. A care worker who finds products left within reach of someone at risk puts them away safely, phones the office before leaving and records a hazard in the incident log; the Care Coordinator speaks to the person or family within 2 working days.

Our own products never stay in a home except our chlorine product and spill kits where the care plan names their storage place; the Care Coordinator arranges their collection when the package ends. Care workers never remove or throw away the person's products without their agreement.

At the medicines assessment under the Assessing Medicines Support Needs Procedure, the assessor checks every medicine against the definition of a hazardous medicine. For any medicine that meets it, or where they are unsure, the Care Coordinator asks the dispensing pharmacist or prescribing team for written advice on handling, PPE, how long body fluids need precautions, laundry, spills, waste and handling by pregnant workers. The advice is recorded in the care plan and risk assessments, and the handling instructions in the eMAR entry, before the first visit at which we give the medicine or handle the person's body fluids, laundry or waste. If written advice has not arrived when a dose is due, the Care Coordinator (On-call Manager out of hours) phones the pharmacist or the prescribing team's advice line, records the advice in the eMAR entry and asks for written confirmation by the end of the next working day. We never give a dose without advice.

bullets: Wear gloves and an apron to handle the medicine, tip tablets or capsules from the pack into a medicine pot without touching them, and wash your hands afterwards. Apply hormone gels only with gloves and do not touch the application site afterwards.
Never crush, split, open or dissolve a hazardous medicine unless the pharmacist's or prescriber's written advice in the eMAR says so.
Wear gloves and an apron for urine, faeces, vomit, soiled pads and linen for the period in the written advice. Where none has been given, apply these precautions for 7 days after the last dose.
Close the toilet lid and flush twice after emptying body fluids, and handle soiled linen and waste as the advice and the infection control procedures set out.
Keep any spill kit the prescribing team supplies where the care plan names it.

blocks.p: A care worker who finds a new medicine that may be hazardous, or hears the person has started one, does not give it, uses gloves and an apron for body fluids, laundry and waste, and phones the office before leaving; advice is then obtained as above before we give any dose. The precautions apply whoever gives the medicine. Where family give it or handle laundry or waste, the care plan records this and the Care Coordinator shares the handling advice with them, with the person's agreement or, where they lack capacity to agree, in their best interests. If a person with capacity refuses, the Care Coordinator gives family the general precautions for body fluids, laundry and waste without naming the medicine, and records this. From the day a worker tells us they are pregnant, have given birth in the last 6 months or are breastfeeding, the Care Coordinator does not allocate them to give a hazardous medicine, handle body fluids, laundry or waste within the precaution period, or clear a hazardous medicine spill, until their individual risk assessment under the New and Expectant Mothers at Work Procedure decides otherwise. A worker planning a pregnancy may ask not to be allocated these tasks, and we agree without asking for reasons.

For a spill of a hazardous medicine or contaminated body fluid, keep others away, put on gloves, apron and goggles, cover the spill with paper towels, wipe it up, then wash the area three times with detergent and warm water, double-bag everything, dispose of it as the written advice and the Waste Management in People's Homes Procedure set out, and phone the office. The Care Coordinator tells the prescribing team the same day.

rows: Unknown powders, liquids or containers, drug-taking equipment, or chemicals suggesting drug manufacture

Do not touch, smell or move them. Phone the office before leaving. If there is a strong chemical smell or you feel unwell, do not go in, or leave with the person if you can, and call 999. Needles follow the Sharps Safety and Needlestick Injury Procedure. The Care Coordinator reviews the home environment risk assessment within 7 days and decides with the Registered Manager the same working day on safeguarding or police involvement.
Pest baits, traps or insect powders
Do not touch them. Record a hazard; the assessor records where they are and keeps care tasks away from them.
Extensive damp or mould

Do not clean it beyond wiping a small area with detergent where the care plan says. Record a hazard; the Care Coordinator tells the person, and with their agreement their landlord, the same working day.
A carbon monoxide alarm sounding, or headache, dizziness or sickness in more than one person in the home
Treat it as serious and imminent danger under the Health and Safety Policy: get everyone out, call the National Gas Emergency Service and, if anyone is unwell, 999.

blocks.p: The On-call Manager can open an electronic copy of our safety data sheets out of hours. For our products, the office or On-call Manager reads the safety data sheet to the care worker or emergency services on request; for household products, the care worker reads the label to the call handler. Give the container to the ambulance crew.

rows: Product in an eye

Rinse with clean, lukewarm running water for at least 20 minutes, holding the eyelid open. Call 999 for bleach, our chlorine product or a corrosive product, and keep rinsing. For a hazardous medicine, or pain, redness or blurred vision after rinsing, go to the emergency department. Otherwise the office gets NHS 111 advice.
Product on skin

Remove contaminated gloves and clothing, rinse with cool running water for at least 20 minutes, then wash with soap and water. Call 999 for blistering, burning or broken skin, as the First Aid Procedure sets out.
A product, or a medicine not prescribed for them, swallowed by anyone
Call 999. Do not make them sick or give them anything to eat or drink. If you are not sure the substance is harmful, call NHS 111.
Fumes breathed in, including from mixed products
Stop, leave the room with the person if you can, and do not go back until the air is clear. Call 999 for breathlessness, chest tightness or a cough that does not settle.
Rash, itching, wheeze or other reaction while using a product
Stop using it, wash the area and phone the office. The product is not used again in that home until the Registered Manager has reviewed it.
Spill of a product

Small spill: gloves, soak up with paper towels, wipe with water and bag the waste. Spill you cannot clean safely: keep people away, ventilate, phone the office and stay with the person in another room; the Field Care Supervisor, or On-call Manager out of hours, attends within 2 hours or agrees how it is cleaned.

blocks.p: Phone the office, or the On-call Manager out of hours, before you leave the home, or at once when you have called 999, and record the event in the incident log before the end of your shift. The office opens the incident log entry from the call, reallocates your later visits if you need to stay or get treatment, and sends a worker who should not drive by taxi at our cost.

The Registered Manager or Deputy Manager reviews every exposure, reaction and swallowing incident within the initial review timescale in the Incident Reporting, Investigation and Learning Policy (the same working day where treatment beyond first aid was needed), updates the COSHH or home assessment, and decides on a RIDDOR report under the RIDDOR Reporting Procedure, a safeguarding referral under the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure where unsafe storage or another person's actions may have caused harm, a CQC notification under the Statutory Notifications to CQC Procedure, and duty of candour under the Duty of Candour Policy where our care harmed the person.
Everyone who gives care, including Senior Care Workers and Field Care Supervisors, is under skin health surveillance because wet work and gloves can cause contact dermatitis.

rows: Baseline skin check
By a trained Field Care Supervisor within 6 weeks of starting, booked by the HR Manager.
Annual skin questionnaire
Sent by the HR Manager in the month of the worker's start anniversary, completed within 2 weeks and reviewed by the Field Care Supervisor within 5 working days.
Visual skin checks
At the frequency our occupational health provider advises, and more often for anyone with confirmed dermatitis.
Symptoms reported or found

Sore, red, cracked, itchy or weeping skin is reported to the Field Care Supervisor before the next shift and managed under the Standard Infection Control Precautions Procedure, with an occupational health referral within 5 working days.
Breathing symptoms
Wheeze, chest tightness or breathlessness linked to a product: the worker stops using it, and the HR Manager refers them to occupational health within 5 working days.

blocks.p: Responsible persons record results without interpreting them; occupational health decides on fitness and restrictions, and the Registered Manager reviews controls after every confirmed case. A doctor's written diagnosis of occupational dermatitis or occupational asthma is passed to the HR Manager within 2 working days and decided under the RIDDOR Reporting Procedure. A worker with a latex or other sensitisation tells the HR Manager, and the Care Coordinator does not allocate tasks involving that substance; assessors record latex items, such as some continence products, in the risk assessments. Workers must attend checks during paid working time and may see their own health record.

Hand rub, chlorine product and spill kit stock is kept in a dedicated, ventilated cupboard away from heat, sunlight and ignition sources, off the floor, with chlorine products apart from acids. Spilt toner is wiped with a damp cloth, never vacuumed. A cleaning contractor gives the Registered Manager its COSHH assessments and safety data sheets before starting, and keeps its products in a locked cupboard; the Registered Manager checks this every 12 months. The Deputy Manager checks substance storage at the quarterly office inspection.

bullets: COSHH register, assessments, safety data sheets, product summaries and contractor information: the branch health and safety file. Superseded assessments and safety data sheets are kept for 40 years under the Records Management and Retention Policy.

Named household products, storage arrangements, hazardous medicine advice and briefings: the person's risk assessments and care plan, with handling instructions in the eMAR entry; phone agreements to use a replacement product: the daily visit notes.
Exposures, reactions, spills, swallowing and unsafe products: the incident log.
Health surveillance records: the restricted section of the staff record, kept for 40 years from the last entry.
Training: training and compliance records; spot check findings: supervision and appraisal records.

blocks.p: The Registered Manager and Deputy Manager write COSHH assessments using their IOSH Managing Safely training, and the external health and safety adviser checks the assessments at the annual independent audit. At every spot check the Field Care Supervisor checks product use, PPE, storage and kit; using a prohibited or unnamed product, mixing products, or leaving products within reach of someone at risk is a critical item, managed under the Quality Audit and Monitoring Procedure.

blocks.p: Every shortfall gets an action, owner and deadline, tracked at the Health and Safety Meeting until complete. This procedure is reviewed every 12 months by the Registered Manager and approved by the Directors under the Policy Management and Document Control Policy, and sooner after a change in law or guidance, a serious exposure incident, an inspection finding, or when monitoring shows the arrangements are not working.
